Native controls on dot and tube displays

Six controls from ui-feed.dev, rebuilt with HTML-in-canvas. The originals are React components. Here each one is a custom element with a drawable canvas in its shadow root, and inside the canvas are ordinary radio inputs, a <textarea>, a <table>, date and time inputs. The canvas draws those elements at one pixel for each dot of the display, copies that small picture with drawImage() and enlarges it through a mask of dots. I wanted to know if a control could keep its own CSS and its own behaviour and still end up as an LED board, with no getImageData(). Tap, type and use the arrow keys on any of them.

Credit: every control on this page is a rebuild of a demo on ui-feed.dev, and each section links to the original it came from. I worked from the published demos rather than their source: I looked at what each one does, worked out the mechanism and built it again around a native form control drawn by a canvas. The designs and the ideas behind them are theirs.

Cinema showings

A native <select size="5">, which is the listbox the platform already has, drawn as an LED board. The rows, the selection highlight, the arrow keys, type-ahead and the scrolling are the browser's. The rows are built from the element's <option> children, and the sold-out showing is a disabled option.

  2. The element. One <select size> styled with CSS, one dotBoard() call, then an invisible draw that puts the list's hit region over the board.

Station departures

Pagination over a table that stays in the page. The <table> is slotted into a drawable <div> in the canvas, and a page of the board is five clipped draws of that one picture. No row is hidden or moved. The page buttons are <button>s in a <nav>, and each line of the board changes a little after the one above it.

LED message counter

A <textarea maxlength="40"> typed into through the board, and a <meter> that the canvas draws as one lamp for each character. Select some text: the ::selection colours are on the board too.

Flip-dot stars

A rating made of five radio inputs with one name. The canvas puts each radio's hit region over a star and draws every cell of the panel as a disc that turns over when its state changes. Left and right arrows move the rating, which is the radio group's own behaviour.

  1. The markup.
  2. The element. The stars are worked out on a grid. Nothing is drawn of the radios: hit() places them.
  3. put() and hit(). A draw with globalAlpha = 0 still moves the hit region.

VCR timer

An <input type="date">, two <input type="time"> and an <input type="number"> in a form, drawn as a video recorder's on-screen display. Tap a field and type, or use the up and down arrows. The picture is redrawn in bands that drift sideways, with a red and a blue copy either side.

Teletext

A command list: an <input role="combobox"> over a list built from <option> children. Type to filter, move with the arrow keys, choose with Enter or a tap. The four coloured words at the bottom are buttons that filter by group.

How it works

Every control here extends one base class, FeedControl in /lib/ui-feed/kit.js. Its shadow root holds a canvas with content="drawable", and the canvas holds the native elements. The control's own CSS is nested under canvas, so when the API is missing or the context is lost the same elements are shown outside the canvas as unstyled HTML and still work.

Drawing is in design units: a control is designed 360 wide, and the context is scaled so that the same numbers work at any width. The elements inside the canvas are laid out at the design size, and drawElementImage() is given that size, so a narrower canvas draws them smaller and their hit regions follow.

The dot board has three steps. The paint handler sets a transform that makes one cell of the design one device pixel, and draws the elements with it, so the browser rasterises the text at one pixel a dot. That corner of the canvas is copied to a small plain canvas with drawImage(). The copy is enlarged with smoothing off into a second plain canvas, a pattern of discs is applied with destination-in, and the result is drawn back. Nothing is read with getImageData(). The reduced draw leaves each element's hit region in that corner, so the last step is a draw with globalAlpha = 0 at the place the board shows it.

Data that an author supplies is light DOM. Four of the controls read <option> children or attributes and build their own inputs. The departures board is different: its table is slotted, drawn as it is, and styled by the page. A control's value reaches its form through ElementInternals.setFormValue(). The line under each demo is the FormData of the form around it.

Live checks

Findings

  • A reduced drawElementImage() is a usable per-dot picture. Text drawn at one device pixel for each dot, copied out and enlarged with smoothing off, read as a dot display from about 7 dots of cap height. Below that the letters ran together.
  • The control's CSS states show on the board with no extra code. The inverted row is label:has(:checked), the dimmed row is :has(:disabled), the yellow frame is :focus-visible, and a text selection in the textarea is drawn in its ::selection colours.
  • The hit region follows the last draw, at any alpha. The list is drawn reduced in a corner first, then once more with globalAlpha = 0 at the board's place. The taps in the checks below land on the right row.
  • A slotted table can be paged without touching it. Twelve rows, five to a page: each line is a clipped draw of the slot's wrapper. The rows keep their layout, so offsetTop of a row is where to clip.
  • A shadow tree can't style slotted cells. ::slotted(table) reaches the table and inherited properties reach the cells. Column widths and the header alignment had to come from the page's stylesheet.
  • Radio inputs in a shadow root with one name and no form are one group. The arrow keys moved the rating from 4 to 3 in the test browser with no key handler in the element.
  • Date and time fields are edited where they are drawn. A click on the drawn minutes field focused that field and typed digits went into it, through the pixelated picture.
  • The text caret wasn't in the picture of the textarea in the test browser, with caret-shape: block or without. The message counter draws its own block cursor. It finds the place with a hidden copy of the text up to the caret, laid out in the same font and width.
  • A <form> in a shadow root's HTML is dropped when the host is inside a form. The parser doesn't nest forms, and innerHTML on the shadow root counts the host's form. My first version of four of these controls had an inner <form> and worked until I put one in a form. They use a <div> now.
  • Not verified: everything on a phone. The native date and time pickers that Android opens for these inputs, the on-screen keyboard over the teletext input, and the frame rate of the VCR picture, which redraws every frame while it is on screen.
